blocks.content: Picture the analytics team at an online store. They want to know yesterday's revenue by category, broken down by region. Where do they think to get that number from?
The obvious answer is the production database, the same one that is powering checkout right now. That answer turns out to be a bad one, and figuring out why leads straight to ETL pipelines.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396326750-446428955.png
blocks.alt: Extract, transform, and load moving data from source systems into a warehouse

blocks.content: An ETL pipeline pulls data out of the systems that create it, reshapes that data into something usable, and lands it somewhere built for asking questions like the one above. Extract, transform, load. Three words, three stages, and together they are the backbone of almost every reporting and analytics system you will ever touch.

You do not need to be a data engineer to run into this. Anyone building a dashboard, a report, or a feature set for a machine learning model eventually hits the same wall, and ETL or its close cousin ELT is the standard answer.
1. What ETL Actually Is

ETL stands for extract, transform, load, and the name is literally the three steps in order. Each stage does one job, and keeping the jobs separate is what makes the whole pipeline manageable instead of a tangled mess.
["Extract pulls raw data out of a source system","Transform cleans, reshapes, and enriches that raw data","Load writes the finished result into a destination built for analytics"]
items: Extract pulls raw data out of a source system
Transform cleans, reshapes, and enriches that raw data
Load writes the finished result into a destination built for analytics

blocks.title: The one line version
blocks.content: ETL takes data that lives where it was created and moves a clean copy of it to where people actually need to analyze it.
1.1 Extract

Extract means pulling raw data out of wherever it currently lives. That could be a production Postgres database, a third party API from a payments provider, or a pile of log files sitting in object storage.

The extract step does not clean anything up yet. Its only job is to get data out of the source system and into the pipeline, reliably, and without disrupting whatever else that source system is busy doing.
1.2 Transform

This is where the real work happens. Raw data is messy. Fields are named inconsistently across systems, values go missing, timestamps show up in different time zones, and the overall shape rarely matches what a report actually needs.

Transform cleans, reshapes, validates, and enriches the data. Cleaning fixes obvious problems like nulls and duplicate rows. Reshaping turns nested or wide data into the flat tables a warehouse prefers. Enriching adds context, like turning a country code into a readable country name.

["Cleaning removes bad rows and fixes obvious data quality issues","Validating checks that values fall within expected bounds before they land anywhere","Reshaping flattens or joins data into the structure a report needs","Enriching adds context the source system never stored in the first place"]
items: Cleaning removes bad rows and fixes obvious data quality issues
Validating checks that values fall within expected bounds before they land anywhere
Reshaping flattens or joins data into the structure a report needs
Enriching adds context the source system never stored in the first place

blocks.content: 1.3 Load
Load takes the transformed data and writes it into its destination, almost always a data warehouse built for fast analytical queries, things like Snowflake, BigQuery, or Redshift.

A good load step is careful about how it writes. Appending blindly creates duplicates the moment a job reruns after a hiccup, so most loads either upsert by a key or overwrite a whole partition of data instead.

blocks.title: Appending is not enough
blocks.content: A load that only appends rows will create duplicates the moment you rerun the job after a failure. Production loads upsert by key or overwrite a partition instead, so a rerun is safe.
2. Why Not Just Query Production

It is tempting to skip all of this and point a BI tool straight at the production database. For a five person startup that can be fine for a while. At any real scale it turns into a problem, for two separate reasons.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396326751-144854649.png
blocks.alt: Production database serving app users while a separate warehouse serves analysts

blocks.content: 2.1 Analytical Queries Are Expensive

A production database is tuned for lots of small, fast operations: fetch this user, update that order, insert one row. An analytical query is the opposite. It might scan millions of rows to compute a monthly total, which takes real time and real CPU.

Run that kind of query against the same database that is serving checkout, and you slow down the exact system real users depend on. One analyst running a slow report can degrade the experience for everyone else.

blocks.title: Do not let reports slow down checkout
blocks.content: Production traffic wants many fast row lookups. Analytics wants scans over millions of rows. Mixing both workloads on one database means one of them starves the other.
2.2 The Schema Is Shaped Wrong

Even if performance were not an issue, a production schema is usually normalized for writing consistent application data, not for answering business questions. Getting revenue by category and region might mean joining across five or six tables every single time.

A warehouse instead stores data pre joined and reshaped into wide, denormalized tables built for exactly the questions analysts ask. That reshaping is precisely what the transform step of ETL exists to do.
3. ETL vs ELT
Where the transform step actually happens is the difference between two closely related patterns, ETL and its more modern cousin ELT.
3.1 Traditional ETL
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396326752-653711073.png
blocks.alt: ETL transforms data before loading it into the warehouse

blocks.content: In classic ETL, data is transformed before it ever reaches the warehouse. A separate transform engine, often something like Spark, cleans and reshapes the data, and only the finished, warehouse ready result gets loaded.

This keeps the warehouse simple and keeps messy raw data out of it entirely. The tradeoff is that all the transform logic lives outside the warehouse, on its own compute, which you have to build and operate.
3.2 The ELT Variant
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396326752-953319843.png
blocks.alt: ELT loads raw data first, then transforms it using the warehouse's own compute

blocks.content: ELT flips the order. Raw data is loaded into the warehouse first, untransformed, and only then is it transformed, using the warehouse's own compute to run the transformation logic as SQL.

ELT became popular once cloud warehouses like Snowflake and BigQuery got powerful and cheap enough to absorb heavy transform workloads themselves. Instead of standing up a separate transform cluster, you just write SQL models and let the warehouse do the crunching.

{"headers":["Aspect","ETL","ELT"],"rows":[["Where transform happens","A separate transform engine before load","Inside the warehouse after load"],["What lands first","Only clean, transformed data","Raw, untransformed data"],["Typical tool","Spark or a custom transform service","dbt running SQL models in the warehouse"],["Good fit for","Limited warehouse compute, strict rules before load","Powerful cloud warehouses, fast iteration"]]}

blocks.title: dbt lives in the T of ELT
blocks.content: dbt lets you write transformations as version controlled SQL models that run using the warehouse's own compute. It is a big part of why ELT became so approachable.
4. Batch Scheduling vs Streaming Ingestion
There is a second independent choice sitting underneath ETL or ELT: how often the pipeline runs at all.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396326753-585472915.png
blocks.alt: A nightly batch job pulling data on a fixed schedule

blocks.content: 4.1 Batch ETL
Most pipelines run on a schedule, nightly or hourly, pulling everything that changed since the last run. This is simple to build, easy to reason about, and cheap to operate.

["Runs on a fixed schedule, commonly once a night","Processes a whole batch of changes at once","Simple to build, debug, and rerun if something goes wrong","Data can be up to a day stale by the time anyone looks at it"]
items: Runs on a fixed schedule, commonly once a night
Processes a whole batch of changes at once
Simple to build, debug, and rerun if something goes wrong
Data can be up to a day stale by the time anyone looks at it

blocks.content: 4.2 Streaming Ingestion
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396326753-444338806.png
blocks.alt: Events flowing continuously into the warehouse through a streaming path

blocks.content: Streaming ingestion instead feeds the pipeline continuously, as events happen, so the warehouse stays close to real time. This costs more in moving parts, ordering, and failure handling than a nightly batch job.

blocks.title: Most teams run both
blocks.content: Batch handles the bulk of historical data cheaply overnight, while a streaming path keeps a handful of time sensitive metrics fresh. Few companies pick only one and call it done.
5. A Worked Example: Orders Pipeline
Let's make this concrete with a full pipeline: extracting daily orders from a production Postgres database, transforming them into a clean fact table, and loading them for a BI dashboard.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396326754-251824575.png
blocks.alt: Orders table extracted, transformed, and loaded into a fact table for a dashboard

blocks.content: 5.1 Extracting Orders
The extract step reads only orders created since the last run, using a saved watermark timestamp so it never reprocesses the whole table.

import psycopg2
import json

WATERMARK_FILE = "last_extracted_at.json"

def get_watermark():
    with open(WATERMARK_FILE) as f:
        return json.load(f)["last_extracted_at"]

def extract_orders():
    conn = psycopg2.connect(host="prod-db.internal", dbname="orders")
    cursor = conn.cursor()
    watermark = get_watermark()
    cursor.execute(
        "SELECT id, customer_id, amount, status, created_at "
        "FROM orders WHERE created_at > %s ORDER BY created_at",
        (watermark,)
    )
    rows = cursor.fetchall()
    cursor.close()
    conn.close()
    return rows

blocks.content: 5.2 Transforming Into a Fact Table
The transform step drops test orders, converts amounts from cents to dollars, and derives a clean order date column that the warehouse table expects.

import pandas as pd

def transform_orders(rows):
    df = pd.DataFrame(
        rows,
        columns=["order_id", "customer_id", "amount_cents", "status", "created_at"]
    )
    df = df[df["status"] != "test"]
    df["amount_usd"] = df["amount_cents"] / 100
    df["order_date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["created_at"]).dt.date
    return df[["order_id", "customer_id", "amount_usd", "status", "order_date"]]

blocks.content: 5.3 Loading Into the Warehouse
The load step upserts each row by order id, so a rerun after a failure updates existing rows instead of duplicating them.

def load_orders(df, warehouse_conn):
    cursor = warehouse_conn.cursor()
    for row in df.itertuples(index=False):
        cursor.execute(
            "INSERT INTO fact_orders (order_id, customer_id, amount_usd, status, order_date) "
            "VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s) "
            "ON CONFLICT (order_id) DO UPDATE SET "
            "amount_usd = EXCLUDED.amount_usd, status = EXCLUDED.status",
            row
        )
    warehouse_conn.commit()
    cursor.close()

blocks.content: 6. Orchestrating With Airflow

Someone still has to run these three steps in order, on a schedule, retry them if they fail, and alert someone if they keep failing. That is the job of an orchestrator, and Apache Airflow is the tool most teams reach for.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396326754-61927109.png
blocks.alt: Airflow running extract, transform, and load as a chain of dependent tasks

blocks.content: Airflow lets you describe a pipeline as a DAG, a directed acyclic graph of tasks with dependencies between them. Each of our three functions becomes a task, and Airflow makes sure transform only starts once extract has finished.

from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator
from datetime import datetime

with DAG(
    dag_id="daily_orders_pipeline",
    schedule_interval="0 2 * * *",
    start_date=datetime(2026, 1, 1),
    catchup=False,
) as dag:

    extract = PythonOperator(
        task_id="extract_orders",
        python_callable=extract_orders,
    )

    transform = PythonOperator(
        task_id="transform_orders",
        python_callable=transform_orders,
    )

    load = PythonOperator(
        task_id="load_orders",
        python_callable=load_orders,
    )

    extract >> transform >> load

blocks.title: Idempotent tasks matter more than the scheduler
blocks.content: Airflow will happily retry a failed task for you, but a retry is only safe if the task can run twice without corrupting data. The orchestrator manages scheduling, not correctness.
7. Common Failure Modes
Pipelines that run every night for years will eventually fail in every way a system can fail. A few failure modes show up again and again.
7.1 Schema Drift Breaks Transforms
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396326755-810961068.png
blocks.alt: A renamed source column silently breaking the transform step downstream

blocks.content: Someone on another team renames a column, drops one, or changes what a status value means, and nobody tells the pipeline. The extract step keeps running fine, but the transform code was written for the old shape, and it either crashes or, worse, silently produces wrong numbers.

blocks.title: Add a schema check upstream
blocks.content: A contract check or schema validation on the extract step catches a renamed or dropped column before it reaches transform code, instead of after it has already broken downstream tables.
7.2 Partial Pipeline Failures
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396327869-757177592.png
blocks.alt: A load step failing halfway through, leaving the warehouse half updated

blocks.content: A pipeline loading five tables might succeed on the first three and then fail on the fourth, because of a timeout, a network blip, or a full disk. Now the warehouse is in a state that never existed in the source system, some tables fresh and some stale.

blocks.title: Design for half finished runs
blocks.content: A pipeline that fails after loading three of five tables should leave the warehouse in a state a rerun can safely fix, not one that needs a manual cleanup query at two in the morning.
7.3 Idempotent Reruns
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396327872-691383331.png
blocks.alt: Rerunning a failed pipeline safely overwrites data instead of duplicating it

blocks.content: The fix that runs through all of this is idempotency. If every load is an upsert by key or a clean overwrite of a whole partition, then rerunning the same job twice, or ten times, lands in exactly the same final state.

blocks.title: Reruns should be safe by default
blocks.content: An idempotent pipeline can be run twice, or ten times, on the same input and land in the same final state. That property is what makes retries boring instead of terrifying.

9. When to Reach for ETL or ELT
blocks.text: 9. When to Reach for ETL or ELT

blocks.content: Not every project needs a full pipeline on day one. A tiny startup with one analyst can sometimes get by on a scheduled SQL export for a while.
Reach for an ETL or ELT pipeline the moment more than one person needs consistent numbers pulled from data that lives in a system built for something else.

The signal to watch for is the same one that shows up across most data infrastructure decisions: as soon as freshness, reliability, and more than one consumer all matter at the same time, the ad hoc approach stops being enough, and it is time to build the real pipeline.
10. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This
blocks.text: 10. HLD Interview: How to Talk About This

blocks.content: ETL and ELT pipelines come up constantly in system design conversations, because almost every product with a dashboard or a report has one running behind the scenes.
Separate OLTP from OLAP: I keep analytical queries off the production database, because mixing transactional and analytical workloads on one system makes both slower.
Know ETL versus ELT: I can explain that ELT pushes the transform step into the warehouse itself, which is why it took over once cloud warehouses got powerful enough to do that work.
Plan for failure: I design loads to be idempotent, usually as upserts or partition overwrites, so a rerun after a partial failure fixes itself instead of needing manual cleanup.
Name real tools: mentioning Airflow for orchestration, dbt for transforms, and Fivetran or Airbyte for extraction shows I know the ecosystem, not just the theory.

Tie it to the bigger picture: ETL and ELT pipelines are the plumbing behind almost every dashboard and report a company relies on, which is why the concept is worth knowing even outside a dedicated data engineering role.
